transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Evan Morales (Redwood AE), Sofia Patel (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (CTO, Cinder), Priya Rao (Head of Platform), Derek Wu (SRE), Asha Nair (PM)

Auto summary (auto):
- Discovery focused on reliability, incident tolerance, fallback policies, and multi-region routing for Redwood hosted/dedicated/private options.
- Cinder's key concerns: predictable latency SLOs, graceful degradation during incidents, data residency and KMS requirements, and clear SLA/penalty structure for production payments.
- Next step: share architecture diagram + run cross-region benchmark.

Transcript:
[00:00] Evan Morales: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — I'm Evan, AE at Redwood, with Sofia on the call who'll handle the deep tech.
[00:14] Liam O'Connor: Hi, Liam here, CTO at Cinder. We've got Priya and Derek on with me.
[00:19] Priya Rao: Priya, platform.
[00:21] Derek Wu: Derek, SRE.
[00:23] Asha Nair: Asha, PM working on the inference rollout.
[00:29] Sofia Patel: Great, quick agenda: reliability requirements, current infra, fallback patterns you want, and where Redwood fits (hosted/dedicated/private).
[00:38] Liam: Sounds good. To set context, we run user-facing recommendation APIs, P95 latency target is 200ms for short queries, and we do longer context sessions for chat that can go up to 8s. We care a lot about incident tolerance — rolling outages last quarter hit us pretty hard.
[00:58] Evan: Totally. Can you share the typical traffic profile? p50/p95, rps, percent of long vs short requests?
[01:07] Derek: Roughly 300 RPS at peak, 85% short quick lookups sub-200 tokens, 15% long chat-ish sessions avg 2k tokens.
[01:18] Sofia: Good. For Redwood hosted, we provide curated multi-region endpoints and automatic routing. For Dedicated, you get reserved pools per account — predictable throughput but you manage some of the networking. Private gives you control in your VPC.
[01:34] Priya: Our main question is incident handling. If a region goes down, how do you fallback without spiking latency or e2e errors?
[01:41] Evan: Two main approaches we use: active-active multi-region routing with health checks and graceful failover, or primary-region with cross-region standby and fast DNS or anycast failover depending on customer needs.
[01:53] Derek: Anycast? We use primarily cloud provider load balancers, would that integrate?
[01:58] Sofia: Yes, we can integrate with cloud LB or handle routing in our control plane. In hosted mode we use smart routing — policy-based: latency-first, cost-first, or region-preferred. If a model variant becomes unavailable, the router automatically falls back to a compatible variant (e.g., quantized or smaller model) with a clear policy.
[02:18] Liam: Quantized variant fallback — ok, what's the stats on degradation? Like how often does quality regress?
[02:24] Sofia: Depends on model and task. We surface regression metrics from evals and allow you to pick fallback tiers: same-class model, quantized same model, or a cheaper architecture. We'll run evals on your prompt sets during the POC to show expected delta.
[02:36] Asha: Do you support split traffic and canary rollouts during incidents?
[02:39] Evan: Yes, rollouts are built-in for model versions and routing policies. Canary percentage, automatic rollback on quality or latency regressions, A/B testing as well.
[02:47] Priya: About SLAs: we need committed p95 availability and credits. Do you do granular SLAs per-route?
[02:53] Evan: For Hosted we offer SLA tiers with uptime targets and response time objectives; Dedicated gets stricter SLAs due to reserved capacity; Private is usually contractually defined. We'll send the SLA matrix in follow-up docs.
[03:07] Derek: For Private deployment we need HSM/KMS integration and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. Can Redwood do that?
[03:13] Sofia: Yes — private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and audit log streaming; we integrate with common SIEM endpoints. Hosted can use Redwood-managed KMS, but we support customer KMS for enterprise.
[03:24] Liam: In an incident where a whole region loses connectivity, what is failover time? Our tolerance is sub-60s for detection+failover.
[03:31] Sofia: On our side, detection is typically within 10-30s depending on probe frequency; routing changes can be immediate for active-active, or up to DNS TTL for DNS-based failovers. For sub-60s we recommend active-active with anycast or our data plane routed healthchecks.
[03:48] Derek: Any gotchas with KV cache / prefix caching across regions? We rely on cache hits to keep latency down.
[03:54] Sofia: Good call — cross-region KV cache consistency can be tricky. We do local caches per region with warm-up strategies and prefix cache invalidation. In failover you might see cold starts; we mitigate with pre-warming and intelligent cache replication for hot keys. There's a tradeoff with cost.
[04:12] Priya: If we go Dedicated, will we lose multi-region routing options?
[04:16] Evan: Not at all — Dedicated can span multiple regions with reserved pools in each region. You can choose single-region dedicated or multi-region dedicated. The orchestration layer handles routing policies across your dedicated pools.
[04:27] Liam: Cost question — fallbacks to cheaper models during incidents. Do you auto-switch and charge differently?
[04:33] Evan: You can define fallback policies that choose cheaper model variants when capacity constrained; billing reflects the model used. We also support throttling with graceful degradation and queueing to preserve latency SLOs.
[04:45] Asha: On monitoring — we need token level breakdowns, per-route traces and gating on latency and hallucination metrics.
[04:52] Sofia: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, latency breakdown and per-request traces. For hallucination/quality we'd hook into your evals; you can supply prompt tests and we generate regression alerts.
[05:04] Liam: Security and compliance — SOC2/ISO?
[05:07] Evan: We are SOC2 Type II and have ISO docs; private deployments get additional attestations if required. We'll attach the compliance pack.
[05:13] Derek: Network topology for private — do you support direct connect / dedicated interconnect?
[05:18] Sofia: Yes, private supports direct connect, VPC peering, and DMZ setups. For sensitive customers we recommend private + direct link to avoid public egress.
[05:26] Priya: Is there an example runbook for incident failover? We want to align our oncall playbooks.
[05:31] Evan: Yes, we have runbooks for region failover, model fallback, and capacity exhaustion. We'll share a sanitized example with the next steps.
[05:39] [10:08] -- mid-call technical deep dive --
[10:08] Sofia: Let me walk through traffic flow for active-active: client -> edge -> regional data plane -> model pool. Health checks run per node and aggregated to make routing decisions. If a node fails, traffic is shifted within ms at the edge and rebalanced.
[10:25] Derek: How do you handle in-flight KV cache state for autoregressive sessions when a request gets routed mid-session to another region?
[10:34] Sofia: We keep session affinity where possible; if affinity breaks, we replay a compacted KV snapshot or reconstruct KV from prefix. There's slight token duplication risk and small latency bump, we document the exact tradeoffs.
[10:47] Liam: What about cross-region data residency — some EU users must stay in EU. Can routing honor geo-residency while still providing failover?
[10:56] Evan: Yes, routing policies can be geo-residency aware: prefer EU region, but on incident you can either fail closed (disallow outbound) or allow controlled failover to other region under exception. We surface those policies for compliance sign-off.
[11:10] Asha: For the POC we want to simulate region fail and measure p95 spike and error rates.
[11:15] Sofia: Good — we'll set up a two-region deployment, run synthetic traffic, and simulate node / region fail to measure detection and failover. We'll include long session retention case to measure KV replay cost.
[11:26] Evan: I'll follow up with pricing bands: hosted (pay-as-you-go), dedicated (reserved GPU pools with monthly commit), private (license + infra). We'll call out SLA differences.
[11:36] Priya: On the SLA side, can you commit to credits if p95 exceeds our target during non-exempt incidents?
[11:41] Evan: Yes, that's standard. We'll include SLA wording and exemption categories (force majeure, customer misconfiguration, upstream infra outages).
[11:49] [20:02] Derek: Curious about telemetry granularity — we want 1s resolution for traces during incidents.
[20:07] Sofia: Console offers sub-second metrics for critical paths and configurable retention for traces. We can export raw spans to your tracing backend.
[20:17] Liam: For benchmark, how long should we run? We want steady-state and chaos windows.
[20:22] Sofia: We recommend a 2-hour steady-state, 30-minute spike tests, and a series of chaos windows where we kill region nodes and simulate latency.
[20:31] Asha: Will Redwood help orchestrate chaos tests or we do it?
[20:34] Evan: We'll collaborate — Redwood runs the platform-side simulations; you control client-side traffic. We'll provide scripts.
[20:40] Priya: For dedicated, how do upgrades work — do you support blue-green?
[20:44] Sofia: Yes blue/green or canary with automatic rollback. Upgrades happen per-pool with traffic split; KV cache warming is part of the rollout to avoid cold start cliffs.
[20:55] Liam: Any limitations on model sizes across regions?
[20:58] Sofia: Depends on hardware footprint in each region; some regions may not have the largest GPU types so we surface compatible model variants. We recommend model pinning per-region if you need exact behavior.
[21:09] Derek: If we see a sudden capacity shortfall, can Redwood throttle lower-priority requests to protect SLOs?
[21:14] Evan: Absolutely — request tiers, token quotas, circuit breakers, and graceful queueing are supported.
[21:21] [30:00] Evan: Quick recap and next steps: Evan share docs + pricing, Sofia set up benchmark plan, Cinder provide traffic profile, schedule technical deep-dive.
[30:12] Liam: That works. Any blockers on our side?
[30:15] Priya: Need to review compliance docs and decide on hosted vs dedicated for the POC.
[30:19] Derek: We'll supply the p95 targets and network topology.
[30:22] Evan: Great — we'll get the follow-ups out today.
[30:26] Sofia: One last note — in many incidents customers prefer a policy: try same model in another region first, then quantized fallback, then smaller model; we can codify that.
[30:36] Liam: Makes sense. We'll want to see the expected quality deltas for our prompt set.
[30:40] Asha: Put the benchmark artifacts and config in a shared folder.
[30:44] Evan: Will do. Thanks everyone, we'll be in touch.
[30:48] Meeting ends.

Notes about transcript quality: auto transcription occasionally mislabeled technical terms (e.g., KV cache -> 'K V cash' in a few lines) and some proper nouns. Action items and next steps captured above.
